newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks cattle passports, labels to fight BSE.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks cattle passports, labels to fight BSE.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday proposed cattle passport and beef labelling schemes in a bid to restore consumer confidence after a public health scare over mad cow disease.
The scare erupted in March after the British government said the fatal cattle brain wasting disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) could spread to humans who ate infected beef.
"Consumers have a right to have the all important information about the beef they eat available to them," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in a statement.

"If this identification and labelling system had been in operation prior to the BSE-crisis, it is unlikely that we would have seen the huge drop in beef consumption which resulted from the scare," he added.

Nearly 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef have been bought into European Union stores after demand dropped by up to 30 percent in some member states, notably Germany and Italy, as worried shoppers switched to pork and poultry.
The EU's executive Commission has now proposed to make it compulsory for all cattle be identified by passports and ear tags which will allow them to be traced back to birth.
Details will be recorded on computer data bases and every farmer will have to keep up to date registers.
The Commission decided tougher measures were needed after many member states ignored voluntary rules adopted in 1992 to identify and register cattle.

But beef labelling would be voluntary because a compulsory scheme would require checks and this would take a long time to set-up, greatly delaying implementation, Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely told a news briefing.
The Commission hopes that the labelling and identification schemes, which have to be approved by EU farm ministers and scrutinised by the European Parliament, will start on January 1, 1997.
Some countries, such as Germany, want compulsory labelling saying that otherwise the scheme would be ineffective.
But the Commission argues that if shoppers insist on labelled beef, the industry will quickly oblige.
If the beef industry decides to use labels they must obey strict rules. Labels may include information about the origin of the animal, feeding, slaughter and where it took place.
A "catch-all" provision in the labelling proposal does not allow it to be used as a weapon to boycott beef from any country, Kiely stressed.
"No country can take unilateral action against imports from other member states," he said in response to a question.
